Paragraph:
'Grieving for you, who would no longer have any refuge, he breathed his last on the shores of the holy Sarayu, committing me to tend to your needs. My sin though unpardonable was not intentional; I implore you to forgive me.' Devastated at the news of his son's death, the sage's eyes streamed with tears. Sighing he said, 'In your ignorance you have transgressed. If you had not confessed to it, you would not be alive; your head would have shattered into a thousand pieces. The race of the Ikshvakus, will also now continue, which would otherwise have been destroyed.' Crying piteously for a son, who was their every thing they wailed, saying, 'Who will now protect us, feed us and look after us as honored guests? Without your shelter we too will soon follow you to that abode of death. There I will request Yama to give you back to us and the righteous lord, will surely grant my wish.'

The old couple tearfully performed the funeral rites of their son, who by merit of his penance and service to his parents immediately ascended the heavens. He then came back to console his parents, assuring them that they would soon be with him and the sage said, 'Slay me now, with a single arrow you snuffed out my son's life. What can surpass that pain? May the grief that now consumes me befall you too, causing your death, as it now causes mine! Since you sinned unwittingly, instead of reducing you to ashes here and now, I curse you to die like me, grieving for a son.'
Characters_Involved: The blind old father of the ascetic
The blind old mother of the ascetic
Situation/Problem_Faced: Dasaratha confesses his 'unpardonable' but 'unintentional' sin to the blind parents. The old sage and his wife are 'devastated' by the news of their son's death, experiencing profound grief and sadness  due to the loss of their only refuge and provider. The sage, after a moment of initial anger and acceptance of Dasaratha's confession, pronounces a curse stemming from his overwhelming sorrow.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: The passage highlights the transformative power of confession, preventing immediate, more severe consequences for Dasaratha. It shows the raw, overwhelming nature of parental grief and the sage's deep despair at losing 'their everything.' The curse, while an act of anger management and justice in a cosmic sense, also functions as an act of profound, shared sadness and retribution, ensuring Dasaratha experiences a similar, consuming sorrow.
Outcome/Resolution: The old couple tearfully performs their son's funeral rites, and the son ascends to heaven, returning to console them. The sage, however, pronounces a curse on Dasaratha: to die from grief over a son, mirroring his own suffering. This curse provides a direct karmic link to Dasaratha's later death, solidifying the theme of acceptance of consequences.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Karma Phala (The central concept, where the sage's curse explicitly links Dasaratha's future suffering and death to his current unwitting sin, ensuring he 'reaps the fruit' of his deed.)
Dukha (The pervasive suffering of the old couple upon losing their son, leading to their profound lamentation, and the grief that 'consumes' the sage.)
Papa (The 'sin' committed by Dasaratha, which, despite being unintentional, necessitates consequences.)
Krodha (The sage's initial anger, which transforms into a powerful curse, a channeling of his rage and sorrow into karmic action.)
Moksha/Svarga (The son's immediate ascension to heaven, indicating spiritual liberation and the merit of his penance and filial service.)
Dharma (The implicit understanding that the curse, though harsh, is a form of justice for the transgression of Dharma.)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The passage details the profound spiritual consequences of Dasaratha's 'unpardonable' papa (sin), even if unwitting. The blind sage, devastated by Dukha (suffering) and grief for his son, and recognizing Dasaratha's adherence to Dharma by confessing, transforms his 'Krodha' (anger) into a powerful Karma Phala—a curse ensuring Dasaratha will experience a similar, consuming grief leading to his death. This intricate exchange highlights the inescapable nature of karmic retribution and the spiritual power of righteous indignation, even in profound sorrow.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, this passage showcases the devastating impact of grief and sadness on the old parents, leading to intense feelings of hopelessness upon losing their only 'refuge.' Dasaratha, burdened by immense guilt and self-blame for his 'unintentional' but 'unpardonable' sin, seeks forgiveness. The sage, after processing his initial shock and profound sorrow, channels his immense anger into a curse. This curse, while a form of psychological release for the sage, effectively transfers his own overwhelming grief and the burden of acceptance of consequences onto Dasaratha, setting the stage for his later demise from sorrow over Rama.
